🔴 Hate the mistake, not the mistaken
✍️ Mostafa Malekian

One of the important points in ethics is distinguishing the mistake from the mistaken. You can hate a bad deed, fight against it, and even prevent it from continuing—without hating the human being who committed that mistake.

Why?

• Hating the mistaken targets the person; whereas love for the human being is a prerequisite for reform. If we consider the person our enemy, then reforming them will no longer be our main goal.

• It helps us see our own mistakes too. When we focus on "finding faults" instead of "finding fault-doers," we realize that we ourselves might commit the same mistakes under certain circumstances.

• Emotions do not override rationality. Hatred of a person can impair our judgment and cause us to seek merely punishment or elimination of the individual, rather than correcting a behavior.

• We do not rush to eliminate the mistaken. The goal is not to eliminate the person; it is to stop the mistake and provide the possibility of reform.

This perspective does not mean being passive in the face of mistakes or injustice. You can firmly fight against a wrong behavior, even stop the mistaken person, but your motivation should not be personal revenge or hatred.

Gandhi has a saying that well illustrates this distinction:
"I hate the wrong deed, but I love human beings and do not hate those who do wrong."

Perhaps it is more ethical to say:
Fight the mistake, not the person.

Because if our goal is to reform the world, we cannot exclude human beings from the circle of our love and compassion—even when we must stand against their mistakes.

➖ Excerpt from the lecture series on Applied Ethics - Part Two - On Love and Compassion

A word to students

After the letter from 46 professors of Sharif University of Technology titled "For Sharif" was sent—which was in fact these colleagues' response to the "Letter from the Mothers of Students Expelled from Sharif"—I and at least four other colleagues who, unfortunately, did not have the honor of writing that letter but had signed it, received numerous messages from some students. All of them, while maintaining a polite tone, asked: "What was your feeling as signatories of this letter when the attack on Minab school happened?" and "Why did these professors not issue a statement at that time and condemn it?" This text is a response to those students.

The attack on Minab school and the killing of innocent children is undoubtedly a war crime. I hope that after the war ends, it will be pursued through an official complaint filed by the government and that appropriate compensation will be granted to the victims' families, although receiving compensation will never bring those innocent children back to their families' arms nor cool that eternal grief.

Therefore, the right way to deal with such atrocities is to pursue them through governmental and international institutions, not to have them condemned by this or that group of citizens. If the professors' letter had merely condemned the expulsion of students, it would have been a useless act as well. Instead, this letter contains a specific demand from the university president to review these rulings in accordance with revised procedures.

And now a word to the students who are dissatisfied with this letter and still support the expulsion of a group of their classmates. In my opinion, in any country in the world, the human and moral duty of a citizen is to side with a fellow citizen when they are up against organizations and institutions, to listen to their words, and to demand fair treatment for them, rather than siding with that organization or institution. The reason is very simple: because even an organization like the municipality is powerful enough and, when facing a citizen, does not need the support of another citizen. Even if a student lives in the most democratic country in the world, when it comes to a student versus an organization, ethically one should stand by one's classmate, not by that organization. For a student, being on a committee where another student—their classmate—receives an expulsion ruling is never a commendable act, and perhaps years later, when the fervor of youth subsides, it will bring shame and regret.

entry.title: [hesmashena] The real innovation of this plan lies in five points: The policy unit shifts…
entry.summary:
Source: @hesmashena

The real innovation of this plan lies in five points: The policy unit shifts from "carrier" to "service." Today, gasoline, gas, electricity, water, and transportation are largely managed in separate platforms. The plan says every decision should be measured based on the final output: "one unit of cooling," "one unit of heating," and "one unit of mobility" — with what combination of resources, technology, and cost they are provided. Four sources and three services are placed in a common decision matrix. For example, replacing gasoline with electricity is only desirable if its effect on the electricity balance, power plant gas, air, and network cost is measured simultaneously. This prevents "transferring imbalance from one carrier to another." Price reform becomes a functional contract rather than a financial measure. The price of excess consumption only rises when a real possibility of reducing consumption has been created; in mobility, that means travel options; in heating, controls and equipment; in cooling, low-consumption technology. This is an operational rule, not a slogan. Instead of buying equipment, the government buys "verified savings." Heaters, coolers, motors, buses, or boiler rooms are not the main subjects of payment. Payment is made against cubic meters of gas, kilowatt-hours of electricity, cubic meters of water, peak megawatts, or actually freed fuel. This change alters the financial and incentive model of the program. Three major consumption markets are redesigned simultaneously and complementarily. In mobility: vehicle–energy–time–cost; in heating: building–equipment–control–behavior; in cooling: electricity–water–peak–comfort. Thus, instead of dozens of scattered projects, three national "savings factories" are formed.

entry.title: [hesmashena] This separation prevents the organization from getting bogged down in…

This separation prevents the organization from getting bogged down in implementation details and losing its main mission, which is increasing the overall system's productivity. The ultimate success criterion: The program's success should not be measured by the number of heaters, coolers, buses, or motorcycles replaced. The right measure is the amount of service produced with fewer resources. In cooling: reduced electricity, water, and peak demand against maintained comfort. In heating: reduced gas and winter peak against maintained comfort. In mobility: energy consumed per passenger-kilometer or ton-kilometer. At the macro level, the final indicator is: providing more or better cooling, heating, and mobility with less water consumption, less damage to air and soil, less energy, and lower public cost. This framework can transform the organization's 24-month program from a set of scattered projects into a coherent and measurable policy. In this view, gasoline, gas, electricity, coolers, heaters, boiler rooms, and vehicles are not themselves the "problem"; they are tools for providing three main services with higher efficiency and less pressure on the country's four basic resources.

Education and health in the employment structure
In the European Union, the share of education and health in total employment is about 22 percent. In some Northern European countries, this ratio reaches 30 percent. More than 70 percent of jobs in these two sectors are held by women (approximately one-third of total female employment is in these two sectors).
In Turkey, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea, Algeria, and Tunisia, the share of these two sectors in total employment is about 11 percent, and in South America it averages between 11 and 12 percent.
The share of education and health in employment in Iran, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Bangladesh is about 8 percent. Apart from the role that education and health play in societal self-reliance, individual autonomy, citizenship, and social reproduction, even from an economic perspective, investment in these two sectors is highly effective in economic reproduction and growth. In Iran, input-output tables confirm this impact. Nevertheless, these two sectors in Iran face serious shortages in terms of financing, human resources, and infrastructure. This issue is particularly important given Iran's population dispersion and area. In this regard, this comparison might be interesting: the number of students in Iran is almost twice that of England, and the number of schools in Iran is more than four times. Iran's area is also about 12 times that of England. In Iran, more than 30 percent of students study in private and semi-private schools, while in England it is about 6 percent. However, the teaching staff of the two countries is almost equal.
In Iran, since the late 1980s, these two sectors have been the focus of government downsizing. Layers of the middle and upper classes also went along with these policies. But beyond the issue of government downsizing, the two institutions that are essential both for societal reproduction and economic growth were seen as surplus costs. According to one of the ministers of the first Hashemi government, some economists justified that these two sectors had the largest share of the government budget, and if only a little of these two were handed over to the private sector, the government's budget deficit would reach zero. He says we were "deceived" and accepted, but the more we handed over from these two sectors, the larger the budget deficit became.
Postscript: Education and health are two main areas of social investment, and there is great emphasis on investing in these two areas to face new risks. In successful experiences, due to the related and intertwined issues of these two areas, extensive job clusters have been formed at national and local levels.

🔘The way to tackle inequality
Angus Deaton, winner of the 2015 Nobel Prize in Economics, leads a team at the UK Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) focused on inequality. The fruit of this group's five years of study was published in April of this year; a book called "Challenging Inequalities," published by Princeton University Press, which has been widely welcomed. Martin Wolf says this book has five key conclusions about inequality:
1. Inequality of opportunity is inextricably linked to inequality of outcomes.
2. Redistribution of income and wealth matters, but so does the social status and dignity that comes from shaping one's own destiny.
